items.abstract: The socioeconomic integration of people with intellectual disabilities (PWID) remains a critical and persistent challenge, despite growing institutional commitment to their work inclusion. Although PWID have increasingly gained access to pre-employment measures, the transition from pre-employment to employment remains challenging and underexplored. Scholars have therefore called for more holistic and theory-informed approaches to understanding how to develop and sustain employment pathways for PWID. Adopting an ecosystem perspective and drawing on stakeholder theory complemented by a human-rights capability approach, the study addresses this gap through an exploratory case study of the PWID employment ecosystem in the province of Alpha, Italy. Primary data were collected through 33 semi-structured interviews and 2 focus groups with key ecosystem stakeholders, while secondary data were drawn from institutional reports, regulations, and media sources. Through abductive thematic analysis, the study develops the Systemic Nested Alliances Model, an ecosystem-based framework that conceptualizes how employment opportunities for PWID can be generated, sustained, and expanded by aligning ecosystem actors around shared responsibilities and transition objectives. Building on the model, the study advances business ethics, CSR, and stakeholder theory by reframing PWID employment as a multilevel responsibility distributed across the employment ecosystem.
items.title: Rethinking Ethical Employment Pathways for People with Intellectual Disabilities: A Systemic Nested Alliances Model

items.abstract: Abstract Many philosophers understand logic as a theory of truth preservation that is value-neutral and becomes prescriptive only when combined with external, non-logical rules. In this article, we develop an alternative view informed by recent work in the philosophy of scientific modeling. We argue that certain logical systems, in certain scientific and philosophical practices, are used as normative scientific models: they represent their targets by combining descriptive idealizations with assumptions adopted—and defended—on normative grounds. We propose a practice-based account of normative models in science, according to which the normative character of a model depends on its use in the relevant research practice, and apply it to the case of classical first-order logic, in its uses as a model of correct reasoning. Finally, we show how our proposal opens up a new perspective on several contemporary debates in the philosophy of logic.
items.title: Logic as Normative Modeling

items.abstract: Academic publishing has largely settled one question about generative AI while leaving another unresolved: AI systems are not eligible for authorship, but the boundary between legitimate assistance and authorship-displacing delegation remains unclear. This article argues that these are separate normative questions. Excluding an LLM from the byline does not by itself justify restricting human use to grammar, readability, or other non-intellectual tasks. At the same time, human approval and responsibility are not sufficient for authorship when authorship-defining intellectual work has been delegated. The relevant boundary is therefore between legitimate substantive assistance and authorship-displacing delegation. In conceptual scholarship, legitimate AI-assisted authorship requires a substantial authorship-relevant human intellectual contribution, critical and integrative command of the developing argument, verification and provenance discipline, proportionate disclosure, and final accountability. The article uses the speechwriter dilemma, peer review, philosophical dialogue, genealogy, and extended cognition to clarify why substantial non-author contribution need not displace human authorship, while still preserving the credit function of the byline. It concludes with a three-level governance model and applies the account reflexively to the article’s own AI-assisted revision process.
items.title: Beyond blanket prohibition: generative ai, accountable authorship, and the genealogy of thought

items.abstract: Sometimes, after evaluating our motivations, values, and goals, we may retain or reject old ones, adopt new ones, and work to fulfill them. As a result, we might gain a skill, shift our perspective on a political issue, or begin to appreciate an aesthetic value. This process is one of active self-shaping. Philosophers have identified a special phenomenon of it through the lens of aspiration and explored its cognitive and conative aspects. Yet, more remains to be said about why we should understand it as a comprehensive experience, one that captures not only both components but also the specific way in which they co-occur, and its continuous nature. In this paper, I aim to provide new grounds for existing discussions and develop and defend three core ideas about aspiration: it is something continuous; incorporates both cognitive and conative elements; and involves an alignment between the two.
items.title: The Aspiration of a Future Death Metal Fanatic

items.abstract: This article develops a framework of normative complementarity for understanding the relationship between charity and justice. Rather than treating charity as reducible to justice or as a substitute for institutional reform, it argues that justice and charity constitute distinct but interdependent domains of moral evaluation. Justice has structural priority because it concerns the principles and institutions governing rights, opportunities, social cooperation, and the distribution of social goods and burdens; charity retains irreducible normative significance because it responds to particular vulnerability, suffering, and urgent need. Drawing on Rawlsian justice, Kantian deontology, utilitarianism, and virtue ethics, the article shows how different traditions illuminate distinct dimensions of this relationship without fully integrating institutional and interpersonal normativity. It further argues that the boundary between justice and charity is permeable: particular practices may embody both dimensions, especially under non-ideal conditions. Attention to moral psychology and global responsibility also demonstrates that charity can foster solidarity and moral formation while risking dependency and paternalism. Normative complementarity therefore preserves the structural priority of justice without treating it as normatively exhaustive, while preventing charity from becoming a substitute for institutional justice.
items.title: Reconsidering Charity in Relation to Social Justice: An Argument for Normative Complementarity

items.abstract: Abstract This paper develops an axiomatic framework for a non-referential theory of meaning by formally characterizing intra-theoretical synonymy through inferential and syntactic criteria rather than through reference or truth conditions. Building on formalist and inferentialist traditions, a series of axioms are proposed that satisfy basic semantic principles such as theory-dependence, semantic holism, and (restricted) compositionality. The resulting systems ( TS 0 and its extensions) satisfy these principles to progressively greater degrees, yielding a sufficiently fine-grained notion of synonymy. The framework thus shows that equality of meaning can be characterized in non-referential terms, while illuminating the limits of non-referential meaning.
items.title: Towards a non-referential theory of meaning: intra-theoretical synonymy

items.abstract: Abstract Some people are safe from harm yet remain in positions where things could easily go badly for them. Their proximity to worlds where something bad happens to them makes their situation ethically precarious. In some worlds, they are excluded, punished, or abandoned, which deserves attention in its own right. We argue that this is not just a matter of risk or harm, but about how people are placed within the space of possible worlds. We explain this through a modal account of difference-making and use it to highlight attitudinal responses fitting to fragility and introduce duties of modal security: moral reasons to protect one another from positions where small changes could lead to significant loss.
items.title: Fragile lives and moral duties: on the ethics of modal security

items.abstract: Abstract Metaphors in science communication do more than simplify complex ideas; they impose certain epistemic frameworks with the potential to steer public attitudes and behavior. In this paper, we investigate the effects of metaphorical framing on public understanding and evaluation of de-extinction, a field where dominant metaphors (“resurrection,” “bringing back to life”) have been criticized for mischaracterizing the technology and fostering undue optimism. We presented a nationally representative sample of the Spanish population ( N = 1,522) with popular science descriptions of de-extinction that varied only in metaphorical framing and assessed its downstream effects on misinformation, perceived scientific rigor, attitudes, funding preferences, and sharing intentions. Promotional metaphors increased misinformation relative to the neutral condition, while critical metaphors reduced it. These effects occurred without altering readers’ perception of the text’s scientific rigor—a dissociation we characterize as credibility without comprehension . Critical metaphors also reduced support for de-extinction, whereas promotional metaphors did not boost support above baseline levels in the neutral condition. Funding allocations and sharing intentions, though related to misinformation, were unaffected by metaphorical framing. We propose that metaphors function as epistemic conditioning devices : they influence downstream judgments not through direct persuasion, but by structuring the understanding upon which those judgments are formed. These findings bear on philosophical debates about the role of metaphors in science, the epistemic preconditions of democratic engagement with emerging technologies, and the limits of lexical precision as a remedy for public misinformation.
items.title: De-extinction, resurrection and biological Frankensteins: scientific metaphors and their impact on public perception

items.abstract: Abstract In the field of mental health, the role of Experts by Experience (ExE) has been gaining increasing attention. However, theoretical research on this topic remains limited, leaving it unclear how ExE can contribute to improving psychiatric research and services. In this paper, I propose two explanations for the contributions of ExE, drawing on perspectives from feminist philosophy of science. The first explanation focuses on the epistemic capabilities of ExE, grounded in standpoint theory. This approach highlights the unique individual potential of ExE as a factor that enhances psychiatric research and services. The second explanation underscores the epistemic diversity between ExE and professionals in research and/or service contexts, focusing on the value of epistemic diversity within teams and communities. The main difference is that epistemic capabilities focus on the individual, while epistemic diversity focuses on the collective. I argue that these two explanatory models should be chosen based on research design, but in the context of psychiatric PPI, considering ExE participation not only in terms of standpoint but also in terms of epistemic diversity may suggest a more inclusive approach to PPI.
items.title: Two explanations of experts by experience in psychiatry: epistemic capabilities or epistemic diversity

items.abstract: Healthcare institutions assessing clinical artificial intelligence (AI) must turn ethical principles, evidence standards and implementation guidance into decisions about specific systems in specific contexts. This paper proposes the Implementation Decision-Tool for Ethical AI (IDEA), an author-developed normative framework for clinical governance committees. IDEA organises assessment across 10 domains and 3 item-level priority tiers: Tier 1 blockers, Tier 2 concerns that can be addressed through mitigation and Tier 3 opportunities for institutional excellence. A mandatory synthesis then connects these assessments to a documented institutional recommendation. Where unresolved Tier 1 uncertainty rules out clinical implementation, IDEA provides a separate route for governed non-clinical evaluation. It also sets minimum procedures for authority, disagreement, conflicts of interest and decision recording. A worked hypothetical application to published evidence on a real sepsis prediction algorithm illustrates how IDEA is intended to operate under evidential uncertainty. IDEA complements broader institutional governance and implementation processes by giving committees an explicitly ethical structure for judgement and authorisation.
items.title: From principles to practice: an Implementation Decision-Tool for Ethical AI in clinical governance

items.abstract: Lived experience has acquired strong moral and political authority in health debates. Personal testimonies are increasingly mobilised not only to show how health policies are experienced but also to contest scientific evidence and challenge public health decisions. This paper argues that experiential knowledge is indispensable, but that its authority has limits. While a person is the authority on how they experience their symptoms and suffering and on what these mean to them, the causal explanation they give of that experience is a different kind of claim: others can assess it and it may prove wrong. The problem arises when the explanation borrows the authority of the experience. Careful defenders of lived experience already recognise this distinction. The difficulty lies elsewhere: in experiential claims that circulate without the procedures that make them answerable, that is, stating what would count against them, submitting them to others able to assess them, and judging them by standards suited to the kind of claim they make. This occurs in public debate and at times within qualitative research itself, as in self-diagnosis, attributed treatment effects and environmental syndromes. We propose epistemic mediation as an ethical safeguard: lived experience is authoritative for meaning and value but cannot on its own settle causal or population-level questions. Such restraint is a requirement of medical ethics, not a methodological preference.
items.title: Giving voice without guardrails: lived experience and the ethics of epistemic mediation in public health

items.abstract: Undergraduate ethics teaching aims to improve future clinical practice by instilling ethical knowledge, character and awareness. However, whether and to what extent ethics teaching can achieve this can be questioned. This paper reports on how some doctors in their first and second years of practice perceived their undergraduate ethics teaching in the light of ethical challenges they had encountered and discusses what these perceptions reveal about the aims of such teaching. We propose that ethics education can promote ethical knowledge and reflective skills but needs to be framed within an understanding of the personal, professional and systemic challenges that doctors face in early clinical practice and the translational work that is required.
items.title: Structural realities and personal impact: how ethics teaching can prepare students for early clinical practice

items.abstract: Abstract Disabled people continue to experience social exclusion and denial of meaningful belonging despite legal commitments to independent living and autonomy. This paper brings disability studies, legal scholarship and philosophical debates around a right against social deprivation into conversation. We argue that the concepts of social access needs and social contribution needs provide a valuable framework for identifying harms that existing disability rights and human rights approaches often fail to recognise or adequately address. At the same time, rather than simply applying the right against social deprivation to disability, we contend that disability offers a critical lens through which the right itself must be rethought. Drawing on critical disability studies, we foreground interdependence, care, relationality and vulnerability, while exposing ableist assumptions that may shape theorising in this area. Through engagement with disability law and rights frameworks, we explore the potential of this dialogue to reconfigure understandings of rights, responsibility and justice.
items.journal: International Journal of Law in Context
items.title: Disability, relationships and a right against social deprivation

items.abstract: Der Konsum von Online-Pornos, eine relativ weit verbreitete Praxis, hat im Vergleich zur philosophischen Diskussion über die abstrakte Natur der Pornografie und im Vergleich zur Ethik anderer Konsumentscheidungen vergleichsweise wenig philosophische Aufmerksamkeit erfahren. In diesem Beitrag argumentiere ich, dass die Entscheidung für den Konsum solcher Medien eine Mitschuld an zutiefst schädlichen Praktiken impliziert. Angesichts der weit verbreiteten Gewalt und Ausbeutung in der Pornografieproduktion akzeptieren Konsumenten ein erhebliches Risiko, dass das konsumierte Material gefilmten Missbrauch oder Vergewaltigung zeigt. Indem man dieses Risiko durch den Konsum von Pornografie eingeht, behandelt man andere auf eine Weise als Mittel zur persönlichen Befriedigung, die ethisch nicht zu rechtfertigen ist. Im zweiten Teil des Artikels, präsentiere ich ein weiteres Problem des Konsums von Online-Pornografie – unabhängig davon, ob sie gewalttätig ist oder nicht –, da der sexuelle Zugang zu anderen durch den Konsum dieser Medien eine Form sexueller Aktivität darstellt, die den allgemein anerkannten Standards einer sinnvollen (moralisch transformierenden) Einwilligung nicht genügt.
items.title: Sexueller Zugang aus der Ferne Sexual access from a distance
